Medical Necessity 1. Aetna considers myringotomy and tympanostomy tube (also known as ventilation tube and grommet) insertion medically necessary for any of the following indications: 1. Autophony due to patulous eustachian tube; or 2. Barotitis media control; or 3. Children with cleft palate and history of otitis media with effusion and persistent hearing loss; or 4. Cholesteatoma; or 5. Chronic retraction of tympanic membrane or pars flaccida; or 6. Complications of otitis media such as meningitis, facial nerve paralysis, coalescent mastoiditis, or brain abscess; or 7. Otitis media with effusion after 3 months or longer and bilateral hearing impairment (defined as 20 dB hearing threshold level or worse in both ears) (tympanostomy tube); or 8. Recurrent episodes of acute otitis media (more than 3 episodes in 6 months or more than 4 episodes in 12 months) (tympanostomy tube); or 9. Severe otalgia in acute otitis media (myringotomy); or 10. To obtain a culture (diagnostic tympanocentesis/myringotomy) of the middle ear fluid prior to beginning or changing antimicrobial therapy (this may be necessary in situations such as otitis media that has failed to respond to appropriate antimicrobial therapy, or for otitis media in individuals or neonates who are immunocompromised); 2. Tympanostomy tube insertion is considered not medically necessary for children with a single episode of otitis media with effusion (OME) of less than 3 months’ duration; 3. Tympanostomy tube insertion is considered not medically necessary for children with recurrent acute otitis media (AOM) who do not have middle ear effusion in either ear at the time of assessment for tube candidacy; 4. Shim placement in the Eustachian tube is considered medically necessary for the management of a patulous Eustachian tube; 5. Balloon dilation of the Eustachian tube (BDET); 1. BDET is considered medically necessary for individuals 8 to 17 years of age when all of the following criteria are met: 1. The individual has Eustachian tube dysfunction from inflammatory pathology resulting in chronic otitis media with effusion; and 2. fetched_contents.text: CG-SURG-46 Myringotomy and Tympanostomy Tube Insertion Clinical UM Guideline Subject: Myringotomy and Tympanostomy Tube Insertion Guideline #: CG-SURG-46 Publish Date: 04/15/2026 Status: Reviewed Last Review Date: 02/19/2026 This document addresses myringotomy and tympanostomy tube insertion, which are procedures used to decompress and ventilate the middle ear when fluid builds up due to infection, trauma, or other conditions. Tympanostomy tubes are also known by other terms, including grommet, T-tube, ear tube, pressure equalization (PE) tube, vent, or myringotomy tube. Note: For a high-level overview of this document, please see “Summary for Members and Families” below. Medically Necessary: The use of combined myringotomy and tympanostomy tube insertion is considered medically necessary for individuals who meet any of the following criteria: 1. Children or adults with recurrent acute otitis media (AOM) (more than 3 episodes in 6 months or more than 4 episodes in 12 months) with or without otitis media with effusion (OME) who have middle ear effusion at the time of assessment for tube candidacy; or 2. Children with unilateral or bilateral OME for greater than or equal to 3 months with hearing loss greater than 20 dB in one or both ears; or 3. Children with recurrent AOM or OME of any duration when the child is at risk for speech, language, or learning delay or disorder from OM based on baseline sensory, physical, cognitive, or behavioral factors including, but not limited to, the following: 1. Confirmed speech or language delay or disorder. 2. Autism spectrum disorder or other pervasive developmental disorder. 3. Syndromes (for instance, Down) or craniofacial disorders that include cognitive, speech, or language delays. 4. Intellectual disability, learning disorder, or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. 5. Blindness or uncorrectable visual impairment. 6. Cleft palate, with or without associated syndrome; or 4. Children or adults with structural damage to the tympanic membrane (TM) or middle ear, such as cholesteatoma, chronic retraction of tympanic membrane or pars flaccida; or 5. Children or adults with barotitis (barotrauma); or 6. Children or adults with autophony due to patulous eustachian tube; or 7. Children or adults with middle ear dysfunction due to head and neck radiation or skull base surgery; or 8. Children or adults with a severe complication of acute otitis media including, but not limited to: meningitis, intracranial abscess, mastoiditis, or facial nerve paralysis; or 9. Adults with OME greater than 3 months and continued symptoms of aural pressure or hearing loss; or 10. Children or adults with persistent AOM despite at least 2 different courses of recommended empiric antibiotic therapy. The use of myringotomy as a stand-alone procedure is considered medically necessary for individuals who meet one or more of the following criteria: 1. Neonates with otitis media who are either: 1. 16 or fewer weeks of age for full term infants; or 2. Premature infant whose adjusted age (actual age - # weeks premature) is less than 16 weeks; or 2. Individual with acute otitis media and an immunocompromising condition such as cancer chemotherapy or use of anti-rejection medications following a transplant; or 3. Individual who meets criteria for tympanostomy and tube insertion but for whom tube insertion is not feasible due to the degree of ear inflammation. Not Medically Necessary: The use of myringotomy alone is considered not medically necessary when the criteria above have not been met and for all other indications. The use of combined myringotomy and tympanostomy tube insertion is considered not medically necessary when the criteria above have not been met and for all other indications. Summary for Members and Families This document describes clinical studies and expert recommendations, and explains whether certain treatments for ear problems, such as creating a small opening in the eardrum (called a myringotomy) or placement of small tubes through the ear drum (called a tympanostomy tube) to improve the airflow and fluid drainage, are appropriate. The following summary does not replace the medical necessity criteria or other information in this document. The summary may not contain all of the relevant criteria or information. This summary is not medical advice. Please check with your healthcare provider for any advice about your health. Key Information. Myringotomy and tympanostomy tube insertion are treatments used when fluid builds up behind the eardrum. This fluid buildup can be caused by infections, injury, or other problems. Myringotomy in combination with or without tympanostomy tubes are commonly used to help drain fluid buildup and air move in and out of the middle ear and keep it dry. These tubes are also called ear tubes, grommets, or PE (pressure equalization) tubes. Most often, these procedures are used in children, but adults can benefit too. In some cases, doctors may perform a myringotomy without inserting tubes, especially for very young infants, people with certain health conditions, or when the eardrum is too inflamed. The procedures are usually safe and help prevent ear infections, improve hearing, and reduce pain or pressure. Newer tools can let doctors place tubes in a clinic setting without needing general anesthesia. Like all medical procedures, these come with risks and should be used only when truly needed. fetched_contents.text: Tympanostomy Tubes or Medical Management for Recurrent Acute Otitis Media Abstract Background Official recommendations differ regarding tympanostomy-tube placement for children with recurrent acute otitis media. Methods We randomly assigned children 6 to 35 months of age who had had at least three episodes of acute otitis media within 6 months, or at least four episodes within 12 months with at least one episode within the preceding 6 months, to either undergo tympanostomy-tube placement or receive medical management involving episodic antimicrobial treatment. The primary outcome was the mean number of episodes of acute otitis media per child-year (rate) during a 2-year period. Results In our main, intention-to-treat analysis, the rate (±SE) of episodes of acute otitis media per child-year during a 2-year period was 1.48±0.08 in the tympanostomy-tube group and 1.56±0.08 in the medical-management group (P=0.66). Because 10% of the children in the tympanostomy-tube group did not undergo tympanostomy-tube placement and 16% of the children in the medical-management group underwent tympanostomy-tube placement at parental request, we conducted a per-protocol analysis, which gave corresponding episode rates of 1.47±0.08 and 1.72±0.11, respectively. Among secondary outcomes in the main analysis, results were mixed. Favoring tympanostomy-tube placement were the time to a first episode of acute otitis media, various episode-related clinical findings, and the percentage of children meeting specified criteria for treatment failure. Favoring medical management was children’s cumulative number of days with otorrhea. Outcomes that did not show substantial differences included the frequency distribution of episodes of acute otitis media, the percentage of episodes considered to be severe, and antimicrobial resistance among respiratory isolates. Trial-related adverse events were limited to those included among the secondary outcomes of the trial. Conclusions Among children 6 to 35 months of age with recurrent acute otitis media, the rate of episodes of acute otitis media during a 2-year period was not significantly lower with tympanostomy-tube placement than with medical management. (Funded by the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders and others; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02567825.) Next to the common cold, acute otitis media is the most frequently diagnosed illness in children in the United States. Clinical justification for prior authorization

The child-level clinical indication for ear tubes is recurrent acute otitis media (AOM) with evidence of persistent middle ear effusion at the time of assessment. The evidence indicates that tympanostomy tubes are typically indicated for children with recurrent AOM, especially when middle ear effusion is present in at least one ear, and for children with otitis media with effusion (OME) that is likely to persist or is associated with hearing loss [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F3]. A key distinction is that recurrent AOM alone without concurrent middle ear effusion is not a sufficient indication by itself; the presence of effusion matters [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-F3].

Recurrent otitis media meets medical necessity because it is the principal indication for tympanostomy-tube placement in children, and the procedure is medically necessary when the child has recurrent AOM with middle ear effusion at the time of assessment for tube candidacy [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-F3]. The evidence base is mixed, with some trials showing no significant long-term reduction in AOM episodes compared to medical management, but also noting that acute otitis media–free periods are commonly observed after surgery [N2-F3]. This creates a nuanced medical necessity context: the procedure is appropriate when the child’s history of recurrent AOM is accompanied by persistent effusion or hearing loss, and when the risks of continued symptoms outweigh the risks of surgery [N2-F3][N2-R5][N1-F1].

Expected benefit versus risk: the main benefit of tympanostomy tubes is improvement in hearing and symptom relief, particularly in the short term, and the possibility of reducing episodes of acute otitis media or preventing complications [N2-F3][N1-F1]. However, the evidence also highlights risks and possible late sequelae, including otorrhea, tube blockage, premature extrusion, structural tympanic-membrane sequelae, and mild conductive hearing loss [N2-F3]. The procedure is therefore appropriate when the child’s recurrent AOM is severe enough that the burden of illness, plus the risk of complications such as hearing impairment or persistent effusion, makes surgery a reasonable option [N2-F3][N1-F1].

Overall, the authorization request should emphasize that the child has recurrent AOM with effusion or other established indications, not just isolated recurrent episodes, and that the procedure is medically necessary because the clinical scenario meets the documented criteria for tympanostomy tube placement while avoiding overuse in non-indicated cases [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-F3].

The main benefits are improved hearing and symptom relief, particularly in the short term, and the potential reduction in episodes of acute otitis media or prevention of complications [N2-F3][N1-F1]. The evidence also highlights risks and possible late sequelae, including otorrhea, tube blockage, premature extrusion, structural tympanic-membrane sequelae, and mild conductive hearing loss [N2-F3]. The procedure is therefore appropriate when the child’s recurrent AOM is severe enough that the burden of illness, plus the risk of complications such as hearing impairment or persistent effusion, makes surgery a reasonable option [N2-F3][N1-F1].

## 2) What documentation the authorization request must include

The authorization request must include **medical records detailing the history and physical examination notes**, plus relevant specialty documentation that supports the indication [N1-F1]. For children, this typically includes evidence of recurrent AOM, middle ear effusion, and any relevant hearing or speech/language findings if applicable [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F3]. The branch reports also emphasize that prior authorization is required for certain covered services to document medical necessity, and that requests must follow the payer’s procedures to ensure accurate and timely processing [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 3) How to phrase medical necessity in the request

Medical necessity should be stated **clearly and directly**, using the documented criteria that the child meets. The language should link the child’s recurrent AOM to the presence of middle ear effusion or another indication such as persistent effusion, hearing loss, or at-risk status for speech/language delay [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N2-F3]. A strong evidence-based way to phrase it is:

> “The patient has recurrent acute otitis media with persistent middle ear effusion at the time of assessment for tube candidacy. The procedure is medically necessary to address symptoms and prevent complications.”

The request should avoid vague claims and instead reference the specific clinical indication that is supported by the evidence, such as “recurrent AOM with middle ear effusion at the time of assessment for tube candidacy” [N1-F1][N2-R1].

## 4) Insurance-specific coverage criteria or exclusions

### Aetna
Aetna considers tympanostomy tube insertion **not medically necessary** for children with a single episode of OME of less than 3 months’ duration or for children with recurrent AOM who do not have middle ear effusion in either ear [N1-F1].

### Anthem
Anthem states that combined myringotomy and tympanostomy tube insertion is medically necessary for children with recurrent AOM with or without OME who have middle ear effusion at the time of assessment for tube candidacy [N1-F2]. Anthem also includes coverage for children with unilateral or bilateral OME lasting 3 months or longer with hearing loss greater than 20 dB in one or both ears, and for at-risk children with speech/language delay, autism spectrum disorder, Down syndrome, intellectual disability, and other developmental conditions [N1-F2].

### Medicare
The evidence provided does not include a Medicare-specific coverage criterion, but the general prior authorization and medical necessity framework suggests the request should still follow Medicare’s standard prior authorization process and documentation requirements [N1-R2][N4-R2]. CMS also notes that prior authorization requirements may vary by code, and some durable medical equipment codes may be suspended or subject to specific rules [N1-R2].

### Medicaid
The evidence suggests that prior authorization is required for tympanostomy tubes in many Medicaid systems, and coverage may depend on work-relatedness, an accepted diagnosis, or other payer-specific conditions [N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-F4]. Washington State L&I coverage conditions require prior authorization and specify that coverage is for AOM with complications, immunocompromised individuals, or recurrent AOM with 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 episodes in 12 months plus effusion [N5-F4].

## 5) Exclusions or conditions that may deny authorization

The branch reports show several exclusionary conditions:

- **Aetna excludes** single-episode OME of less than 3 months’ duration and recurrent AOM without middle ear effusion in either ear [N1-F1].
- **Anthem excludes** cases where the criteria above have not been met and for all other indications [N1-F2].
- **Washington State L&I excludes** coverage unless work-relatedness is established and otitis media is an accepted diagnosis on the claim [N5-F4].

These exclusions mean the authorization request must clearly show that the child meets the insurer’s exact indication, or the request may be denied.

## 6) How payer-specific rules affect the authorization request

The request must be **tailored to each insurer’s exact criteria**. If the child has only recurrent AOM without effusion, the request is weaker and may be denied; if the child has recurrent AOM with effusion, hearing loss, or at-risk status, the request is stronger [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. The request should also include documentation that supports the specific criterion the insurer is asking for, such as middle ear effusion, hearing loss, speech delay, or at-risk status [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. In some cases, prior authorization is required for the procedure regardless of the payer, so the request must follow the insurer’s specific authorization process and submission requirements [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 7) Patient-specific narrative and authorization-ready language

### Stable child with no pertinent past medical history
The patient is a **stable child with no pertinent past medical history**, which makes the clinical picture simpler and supports a focused authorization request [N1-F1]. The absence of other significant medical history strengthens the argument that the procedure is being considered for its direct clinical effect rather than for unrelated concerns.

### Clear, concise explanation of the referral and procedure
The referral is for **ear tube insertion** because the child has recurrent otitis media and the clinical team believes the presence of middle ear effusion supports the procedure [N2-R1][N2-F3]. The procedure is intended to relieve symptoms, improve hearing, and reduce the risk of ongoing complications [N1-F1][N2-F3]. The language should be direct and evidence-based, avoiding overly technical detail while still being specific enough to show clinical justification.

### How to package the request for approval
The request should be packaged as a single, focused authorization package rather than a broad clinical narrative. It should include:
- a brief summary of the patient’s stability and absence of pertinent past medical history,
- the specific indication for ear tubes,
- the planned procedure date,
- the medical necessity rationale,
- and any required supporting documentation such as history and physical notes, effusion documentation, and hearing or speech/language findings if applicable [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4][N5-F4].

A strong authorization-ready template would read:

> “The patient is stable with no pertinent past medical history. The child has recurrent otitis media and meets the criteria for tympanostomy tube placement because of persistent middle ear effusion. The procedure is medically necessary to address symptoms and prevent complications. Supporting documentation includes [briefly list the key documents].”

## 8) Final authorization-ready package

Putting it all together, the authorization request should include:
1. **Patient information** (name, age, date of birth, date of the procedure).
2. **Clinical indication** (recurrent AOM with middle ear effusion, or another applicable criterion).
3. **Medical necessity rationale** tied to the insurer’s exact policy language.
4. **Required documentation** such as history and physical notes, effusion findings, and any hearing or speech/language documentation [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-R4][N5-F4].
5. **Authorization language** that is direct, evidence-based, and aligned with the insurer’s criteria [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5].

## 9) Bottom line

Yes, the authorization request can be written, but it must be **evidence-based, insurer-specific, and carefully documented**. The strongest path is to emphasize **recurrent AOM with persistent middle ear effusion**, show that the child meets the insurer’s criteria, and attach the required supporting records [N2-R1][N2-F3][N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. If the child does **not** have effusion or another applicable indication, the request may still be denied, so the evidence and documentation are the most important parts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R4].
